summary: Stone cabin built 1921 by the Dominion Forestry Branch on Eagle Pass Mountain; closed 1931, roof lost before 1975, and a 2016 shelter was set for dismantling.

facts.design: Mortared stone cabin, 3.7 by 3.7 m (12 by 12 ft), with a pyramidal hip roof
facts.status_note: The roof was lost before 1975 and the page describes only the lower stone walls. No source I could read says what is there now.

events.note: Built by the Dominion Forestry Branch, which administered the Railway Belt forest lands
Opened on the peak at 2311 m (7,700 ft) as a lookout
J. H. Aubrey, said to be the first lookout man, is known to have occupied it 1924-1928 at $120 a month
Active until 1931; closed by the impacts of the Great Depression and never reopened
Roof swept away by heavy snow sometime before 1975, leaving lower walls 1.2 m (4 ft) high
Two local enthusiasts built a new shelter on the stone walls; Ministry stop-work order and a $20,000 fine
Rec Sites and Trails BC decided to dismantle the new cabin, scheduled for summer 2022; the page does not say whether this happened

evidence.supports: Location given as Columbia-Shuswap, BC, Canada
Built 1921 by the Dominion Forestry Branch, which administered the Railway Belt forest lands
evidence.quote: Eagle Pass Mountain lookout was built in 1921 by the Dominion Forestry Branch, which administered the forest lands in BC's Railway Belt.

evidence.supports: First of four 12 x 12-foot cabins, mortared stone, pyramidal hip roof
evidence.quote: It was the first of four 12 x 12-foot cabins, built of mortared stone and topped by a pyramidal hip roof

evidence.supports: Senior Fire Ranger Mizon located the trail
evidence.quote: Senior Fire Ranger John "Jack" Mizon of Malakwa located the trail

evidence.supports: Mizon oversaw construction of the lookout
evidence.quote: he also oversaw the construction of the lookout

evidence.supports: 21 km of pack trail, telephone line, overnight cabin halfway along the trail
evidence.quote: involving the construction of 13 miles (21 km) of trail suitable for pack horses (at a cost of $1791) and telephone line ($2254), the lookout cabin ($1380), and an overnight cabin halfway along the trail ($210).

evidence.supports: Opened on the peak at 2311 m (7,700 ft) in 1922
evidence.quote: Eagle Pass Mountain lookout opened on top of the prominent 7700-foot (2311 m) peak in 1922.

evidence.supports: Aubrey said to be the first lookout man; known to have occupied it 1924-1928 at $120 a month
evidence.quote: J. H. "Jack" Aubrey is said to be the first lookout man; certainly he is known to have occupied the lookout between 1924 and 28, earning $120 per month.

evidence.supports: Active until 1931; closed by the Great Depression and never reopened
evidence.quote: The lookout was active until 1931; closed by the impacts of the Great Depression, it never re-opened.

evidence.supports: Roof swept away by heavy snow before 1975; 4-ft lower walls left
evidence.quote: The vacant cabin stood proud until its roof was swept away by heavy snow sometime before 1975, leaving only the 4-foot-high lower walls.

evidence.supports: Visitors hiked or sledded the old pack trail to the ruins
evidence.quote: The ruins were visited by a growing number of visitors that hiked or sledded the old pack trail

evidence.supports: 2016 shelter built on the stone walls; builders believed they had verbal permission
evidence.quote: until in 2016 two local outdoor enthusiasts built a new shelter on top of the stone walls, believing that they had received verbal permission from the Ministry of Forests Lands and Natural Resource Operations (MFLNRORD).

evidence.supports: Ministry stop-work order on the nearly completed structure; one man fined $20,000
evidence.quote: the Ministry issued a stop-work order on the nearly completed structure and fined one of the two men $20,000.

evidence.supports: Rec Sites and Trails BC administers the trail and site; convened a working group to consider all options
evidence.quote: After Rec Sites and Trails BC (the agency that administers the trail and lookout site) convened a working group to consider all options

evidence.supports: Decision to dismantle the new cabin, described as controversial, scheduled for summer 2022
evidence.quote: it made the (again controversial) decision to dismantle the new cabin, which is scheduled for summer 2022.

notes_for_editor: One source: the Firelookout.ca page, detailed but volunteer-written and undated, so the 1921 build and 1922 opening rest on it alone. The fate after 2022 is unresolved and is the priority for a human. Search snippets (pages not opened; the CBC article timed out and WebFetch returned 403; the Burns Lake District News URL returned the site homepage) report a news story headed 'Century-old Eagle Pass Mountain cabin gutted by fire' and another headed 'Rehabilitated historic Eagle Pass Fire Lookout in Shuswap destroyed by blaze', the second citing 'Tuesday, Aug. 2' with no year visible. The story does not mention a fire because no page I could open says so. If a reader can open those articles, add a fate sentence with a quote. A Vernon Outdoors Club snippet says the lookout was originally built in 1922, which conflicts with the register's 1921 build year; not opened. A Sites and Trails BC resource snippet says the lookout is closed and unsafe for public use; that page (REC1934) returned empty and is not used. No source I could read describes current access, so the story makes no visit claims and does not encourage climbing the ruins. The story names the area as Columbia-Shuswap, as the page does; the Regional District name is not on the page, so the story leaves it out.
